To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) feeding at 1600, rather than ad libitum, did not reduce intake or gain, but reduced water intake; 2) sprinkling cattle at midday, rather than at 1400, increased marbling and feed efficiency; and 3) sprinkling cattle in the morning, rather than the afternoon, increased water intake, but reduced marbling and gain.

1) feeding time and sprinkling can be used to decrease the feed intake pattern and heat load of feedlot cattle; however, these strategies did not affect feed intake or cattle performance; 2) feeding at a reduced level during the heat of the day decreased feed intake and improved feed efficiency of cattle; and 3) sprinkling decreased water intake and marbled score of cattle.

feedlot cattle performance was not adversely affected by feeding management strategies that decreased feed intake during the heat of the day and that sprinkling cattle at the time of feeding decreased feed intake but did not affect performance of cattle fed at night.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of management strategies designed to reduce the heat stress of cattle during the summer.
developing and evaluating management strategies to decrease heat stress in feedlot cattle.
the effect of management strategies on heat stress of feedlots.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
feed and water intake were not affected by the management strategies used.
feeding time, feed restriction, and water application have minimal effects on cattle intake and performance during heat stress.
feedlot management strategies designed to reduce heat stress of cattle have limited effects on cattle performance and are most useful for reducing heat stress related mortality.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

feedlot cattle can be managed to reduce the risk of heat stress without adverse performance effects, and that bunk scoring is a useful tool in determining the effectiveness of heat stress mitigation strategies.
cattle fed at 0800 and sprinkled during the day were more resistant to the effects of high temperatures and had better marbling scores.
the most important aspect of managing cattle in hot weather is to provide a continuous source of water and to provide shade.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the feeding time is important to consider when developing heat stress mitigation programs.
cattle will eat more when they can, but if you restrict their access to feed, they will eat less.
feedlot managers should not be overly concerned about feeding at 1600 vs. 0800.
